query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy is governed by the selective oxidation behavior of its constituent elements. Under oxidizing conditions, rapid formation of a coherent, thin Al/Cr-rich oxide scale protects the underlying fcc matrix and preserves mechanical integrity. Under reducing conditions, however, insufficient or non‐protective oxide formation (with possible contributions from Ti and Fe oxidation) leads to internal elemental redistribution and the precipitation of disruptive oxide phases along grain boundaries, causing microstructural degradation and decreased fatigue performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated, additively manufactured fcc high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous elemental distribution and high strength/fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Exposure to elevated temperatures (e.g., 850°C) in atmospheres that are either oxidizing (e.g., air) or reducing (e.g., an H2/N2 mixture).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature near operational limits (around 850°C) for time periods sufficient to allow scale development and elemental redistribution, under controlled oxidizing versus reducing gas compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or lack) of a protective, nanocrystalline oxide scale at the alloy surface and at internal grain boundaries, which mediates the elemental segregation and subsequent mechanical degradation.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing environment, rapid oxidation of Al and Cr produces a coherent, slow-growing oxide scale that passivates the surface and minimizes further degradation. In a reducing environment, the protective oxide scale does not form properly; instead, oxidation proceeds sporadically (involving less effective oxides of Ti and Fe), leading to elemental redistribution at grain boundaries that undermines the microstructural integrity and fatigue properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing conditions will develop a thin, uniform Al/Cr-rich oxide scale with only minor effects on fatigue performance. In contrast, samples under reducing conditions will show irregular, possibly thicker oxide precipitates at or near grain boundaries, accompanied by measurable reductions in mechanical strength and fatigue life.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated high-entropy alloy’s microstructure and mechanical properties (high strength and fatigue resistance) before any high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: Test temperatures around 850°C with well-controlled oxidizing (e.g., air) versus reducing (e.g., H2/N2 mixture) atmospheric compositions; these boundaries separate regimes where the oxide scale is protective versus non-protective.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of oxide formation and elemental redistribution, as well as the influence of additive manufacturing–induced microstructural heterogeneities, remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of identical as-fabricated alloy specimens and expose them for the same duration (e.g., 24–100 hours) at 850°C in two controlled atmospheres: one in air (oxidizing) and the other in a specified H2/N2 mixture (reducing). Then, perform cross-sectional characterization of oxide scale thickness and composition (using SEM/EDS and TEM), measure elemental profiles near grain boundaries, and conduct fatigue and strength tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microstructural characterization and mechanical testing reveal that both oxidizing and reducing exposures result in similar oxide scale formation, elemental distributions, and negligible differences in fatigue performance, or if a protective oxide layer also forms in the reducing environment, the hypothesis would be falsified.
